slides.title: Part 1. Water as a Lubricant and Cushion
slides.body:
Part 1. Water as a Lubricant and Cushion

The majority of your body weight is water, with various uses:
synovial fluid
synovial joints
pleural fluid
pleural membranes
mucus
lining digestive tract, etc.
cerebrospinal fluid
within and around central nervous system

Synovial Joints. Credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Pleura surrounding lungs. Credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Cerebrospinal fluid. Credit: Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". WikiJournal of Medicine 1 (2). DOI:10.15347/wjm/2014.010. ISSN 2002-4436., CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Digestive Tract. Credit: LadyofHats, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The majority of your body weight is water. 

Water is found both within and between the cells of your body. 

This water serves various functions. One function of water is as a lubricant. Normally, we think of oils as lubricating things like door hinges or bike locks, but in your body, it’s water that helps serve this function. Water is a component of synovial fluid, a thick fluid that lubricates synovial joints. Water is also a component of pleural fluid—a fluid that fills the space between two pleural membranes, allowing the lungs to expand and contract without rubbing against other internal organs and causing damage. Water is also the basis of mucus, which is secreted by cells in various parts of the body, including the digestive tract, where it helps lubricate the passage for food. Water also serves as the basis for cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, which is found in openings of the central nervous system, as well as surrounding the brain and spinal cord. One function of CSF is to cushion your central nervous system from physical trauma.

slides.title: Part 1. Water as a Heat Sink
slides.body:
Part 1. Water as a Heat Sink

Water acts as heat sink to absorb heat from your core, and transport it to peripheral capillaries (radiant heat loss) and your skin (evaporative heat loss)
heat is generated from breaking molecular bonds in nutrients and ATP

(~50% of this energy is lost as heat)

Energy release with ATP hydrolysis. Credit: Eunice Laurent, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Cooling from evaporation of sweat. Credit: Wilfredor, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Water also serves as a heat sink, protecting your body from dramatic fluctuations in temperature. A heat sink is a substance that can absorb and dissipate, or scatter, heat without experiencing a significant increase in its own temperature. Water is an especially good heat sink due to the hydrogen bonds between its molecules—recall these bonds from the last unit? These hydrogen bonds necessitate a relatively large amount of energy (including heat) to break them apart from one another.

Your body’s metabolic reactions are constantly generating heat. Whenever you break a bond between atoms in nutrients that you have consumed, some of the released energy escapes as heat. The remaining energy is often stored as ATP for later use, but when you break down ATP to serve some bodily function, you again lose some of the liberated energy as heat. This heat generation is great when you are in a cold environment, but when environmental temperatures rise, you may begin to overheat. Water is a component of your blood that allows it to absorb some of this heat from your body’s warm core and carry it to your body’s outer surfaces. There, heat is released from the body as radiant energy, dissipating from your body tissues into the air. Additionally, water released at your body surface as sweat is able to evaporate, further cooling your tissues and the blood passing through them. This evaporative cooling is due to energy, including heat, being required to break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. The blood that is cooled by this release of radiant heat and evaporation is then recirculated back to your body’s core, where it can again absorb freshly generated heat and transport it away, thus repeating the process.

slides.title: Part 1. Water as a Component of Liquid Mixtures
slides.body:
Part 1. Water as a Component of Liquid Mixtures

In a mixture, the constituent substances are not chemically bonded into a new, larger chemical compound, but rather remain distinct (e.g., air)
e.g., a solution where water is the solvent and sodium and chloride are the solutes
in a homogenous solution, the solutes and solvent are distributed equally throughout

Salt and water. Credit: Chris 73 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Salt dissolved in water. Credit: Hawesthoughts, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Remember how when we began unit 1, we discussed how matter can be found as a pure substance, or a mixture of substances, each of which retains its own chemical identity? If you recall, in a mixture, the constituent substances are not chemically bonded into a new, larger chemical compound, but rather remain distinct. For instance, if you poured sugar and salt onto a table and mixed them together, they would remain sugar and salt—they would not be fused into a new substance. This is also true of the air you breathe—it is not a pure substance, but rather a mixture of different types of gasses. 

Your body also contains mixtures. For instance, the sodium and chloride ions that we discussed in the last unit act as solutes when dissolved within water, a solvent. In general, a solute is something that dissolves in a solvent. In these solutions, the solute is distributed equally within the solvent—that is, the solution is homogenous. In the example we just discussed, sodium and chloride ions are interspersed at regular intervals with water molecules throughout the saltwater solution.

slides.title: Part 1. The Role of Water in Chemical Reactions
slides.body:
Part 1. The Role of Water in Chemical Reactions

Water is produced in dehydration synthesis (also commonly called a condensation reaction), and split in a hydrolysis reaction

Figure 1. Dehydration Synthesis and Hydrolysis.  Monomers, the basic units for building larger molecules, form polymers (two or more chemically-bonded monomers). (a) In dehydration synthesis, two monomers are covalently bonded in a reaction in which one gives up a hydroxyl group and the other a hydrogen atom. A molecule of water is released as a byproduct during dehydration reactions. (b) In hydrolysis, the covalent bond between two monomers is split by the addition of a hydrogen atom to one and a hydroxyl group to the other, which requires the contribution of one molecule of water.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Water also plays a role in your body’s chemical reactions. 

In dehydration synthesis (also commonly called a condensation reaction), water is released when two molecules form a covalent bond. This occurs when a hydrogen molecule from one reactant and a hydroxyl (OH) group from the other reactant combine to form water, and the remaining portions of the reactants become bonded to one another.

A hydrolysis reaction is basically the reverse of this process: a water molecule breaks up a compound, with the water itself splitting into a hydrogen atom and a hydroxyl group, each of which bonds to one of the now split compounds.

slides.title: Part 2. Body Water Content
slides.body:
Part 2. Body Water Content

Your body is 50-60% water
from ~75% in infants to ~45% in old age
women ~50%, men ~60%
The water content of body parts ranges widely

Figure 2. Water Content of the Body’s Organs and Tissues. Water content varies in different body organs and tissues, from as little as 8 percent in the teeth to as much as 85 percent in the brain.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Human beings are mostly water, ranging from about 75 percent of body mass in infants to as low as 45 percent in old age. This difference is due to the change in body composition and nutrient storage across the lifespan. In adults, the average percent of body mass in women is 50%, whereas in men the average is 60%.

slides.title: Part 2. Intracellular and Extracellular Fluid Compartments
slides.body:
Part 2. Intracellular and Extracellular Fluid Compartments

Body fluids divided into intracellular (~55%) and extracellular fluid (~45%)
intracellular fluid is found within cells (cytosol (fluid portion)/cytoplasm)
extracellular fluid subdivisions: interstitial fluid (80%), plasma (16%), other (lymph, cerebrospinal fluid, synovial fluid, pleural fluids, pericardial fluids, etc.)

Figure 3. Fluid Compartments in the Human Body. The intracellular fluid (ICF) is the fluid within cells. The interstitial fluid (IF) is part of the extracellular fluid (ECF) between the cells. Blood plasma is the second part of the extracellular fluid. Materials travel between cells and the plasma in capillaries through the interstitial fluid.

Figure 4. Proportions of Total Body Fluid in Each of the Body’s Fluid Compartments. Most of the water in the body is intracellular fluid. The second largest volume is the interstitial fluid, which surrounds cells that are not blood cells.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
This water makes up the basis of various bodily fluids. We can categorize those fluids by how they are compartmentalized. 

For instance, some fluid, referred to as cytosol or cytoplasm, is located within cells and therefore referred to as intracellular fluid. Intracellular fluid makes up about 55% of the water in your body. This volume is very stable because the water content of cells is closely regulated – too little water and the cells shrink… too much, and they may burst.

The remaining 45% of water in your body is found outside of cells. Of this extracellular fluid, the majority is interstitial fluid—the fluid surrounding living cells. Interstitial fluid comprises about 80% of the extracellular fluid total, and thus 36% of the water in your body. 

About 16% of your extracellular fluid, or 7% of your overall water content, comprises plasma—the fluid portion of your blood. Plasma transports a range of materials, including blood cells, electrolytes, nutrients, gases, wastes, and proteins (which include substances such as clotting factors, antibodies, and hormones). Gases, nutrients, and waste materials travel between capillaries, your smallest blood vessels, and cells through the aforementioned interstitial fluid. Cells are separated from the interstitial fluid content by a selectively permeable cell membrane that helps regulate the passage of materials between the interstitial fluid and the interior of that cell. We’ll talk a lot about these processes later in the course.

Other extracellular fluids include the cerebrospinal fluid of the brain and spinal cord, the lymph (which is excess interstitial fluid that has drained out of the bloodstream and is being returned to the blood through lymphatic vessels), the aforementioned synovial and pleural fluids, as well as pericardial fluid in the cardiac sac, and many others. Please note that the pericardial fluid serves a similar function to pleural fluid: allowing the heart to contract and expand without rubbing against other organs.

slides.title: Part 2. Composition of Body Fluids
slides.body:
Part 2. Composition of Body Fluids

Extracellular fluids are similar to one another
e.g., plasma and interstitial fluid 
Extracellular fluids are not similar to intracellular fluid

The Concentrations of Different Ions in Key Bodily Fluids. The graph shows the composition of the intracellular fluid and extracellular fluid (interstitial fluid and plasma). The compositions of plasma and interstitial fluid are similar to one another but are quite different from the composition of the intracellular fluid.
slides.notes:
The compositions of two components of the extracellular fluid—plasma and interstitial fluid—are more similar to each other than either is to intracellular fluid. Both blood plasma and interstitial fluid have high concentrations of sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate ions. Interstitial fluid, which is derived from plasma, just lacks the relatively high concentration of proteins found in the plasma as those proteins do not leak out of capillaries as do the smaller components of plasma that are the basis for interstitial fluid. We’ll cover proteins in more detail in the next unit, so this concept will become clearer. 

In contrast, intracellular fluid has elevated amounts of potassium, phosphate, and magnesium ions, as well as proteins.

slides.title: Part 2. Composition of Body Fluids
slides.body:
Part 2. Composition of Body Fluids

Body fluids are neutral in charge
cations and anions balance one another both inside and outside of cells
In extracellular fluid: primarily sodium (Na+) ions and chloride (Cl–) ions
In intracellular fluid: primarily potassium (K+) ions and phosphate ions (HPO42-) (the latter also occurs in the PO43- form, but the former is more common in body fluids)
High extracellular Na+ and intracellular K+ concentrations are maintained by sodium-potassium pumps

The Sodium-Potassium Pump. The sodium-potassium pump is powered by ATP to transfer sodium out of the cytoplasm and into the extracellular fluid. The pump also transfers potassium out of the extracellular fluid and into the cytoplasm. (credit: modification of work by Mariana Ruiz Villarreal).
slides.notes:
Body fluids are neutral in charge. Thus, cations, or positively charged ions, and anions, or negatively charged ions, are balanced in fluids. As seen in the previous graph, sodium (Na+) ions and chloride (Cl–) ions are concentrated in the extracellular fluid of the body, whereas potassium (K+) and phosphate (HPO42-) ions are concentrated inside cells. 

Although sodium and potassium can “leak” through “pores” into and out of cells, respectively, the high levels of potassium and low levels of sodium in the intracellular fluid are maintained by sodium-potassium pumps in the cell membranes. These pumps use the energy supplied by ATP to pump sodium out of the cell and potassium into the cell.

slides.title: Part 2. Roles of Electrolytes
slides.body:
Part 2. Roles of Electrolytes

Key functions of ions and electrolytes (ion-containing solutions):
electrical signalling in neurons and muscles
aiding water movement in body using osmosis
stabilize protein structures
aid in releasing hormones from glands
strengthening bones and teeth
slides.notes: The body contains a large variety of ions, or electrolytes, which perform a variety of functions. Some—especially sodium and potassium ions—assist in the transmission of electrical impulses along cell membranes in neurons and muscles. Other ions help to stabilize protein structures in enzymes. Still others aid in releasing hormones from endocrine glands. Calcium and phosphate that enter the body are incorporated into bones and teeth. All of the ions in plasma contribute to the osmotic balance that controls the movement of water between cells and their environment.

slides.title: Part 3. Acid-Base Balance
slides.body:
Part 3. Acid-Base Balance

Acids and bases, like salts, dissociate in water into electrolytes
An acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions (H+) in solution
hydrogen (H) has 1 proton and 1 electron (most common isotope has no neutrons)
H+ has just one proton (having lost electron)
hence, H+ referred to as a “proton”

Acids and Bases. (a) In aqueous solution, an acid dissociates into hydrogen ions (H+) and anions. Nearly every molecule of a strong acid dissociates, producing a high concentration of H+. (b) In aqueous solution, a base dissociates into hydroxyl ions (OH–) and cations. Nearly every molecule of a strong base dissociates, producing a high concentration of OH–.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Acids and bases, like salts, dissociate in water into electrolytes. Acids and bases can very much change the properties of the solutions in which they are dissolved.

An acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions (H+) in solution. Because an atom of hydrogen has just one proton and one electron, a positively charged hydrogen ion is simply a proton. This solitary proton is highly likely to participate in chemical reactions.

slides.title: Part 3. Acid-Base Balance
slides.body:
Part 3. Acid-Base Balance

Strong acids are those that release all of their H+ in solution
e.g., HCl
Weak acids do not release H+ from all molecules (do not ionize completely)
e.g., acetic acid (vinegar)

Acids and Bases. (a) In aqueous solution, an acid dissociates into hydrogen ions (H+) and anions. Nearly every molecule of a strong acid dissociates, producing a high concentration of H+. (b) In aqueous solution, a base dissociates into hydroxyl ions (OH–) and cations. Nearly every molecule of a strong base dissociates, producing a high concentration of OH–.
slides.notes: Strong acids are compounds that release all of their H+ in solution; that is, they ionize completely. Hydrochloric acid (HCl), which is released from cells in the lining of the stomach, is a strong acid because it releases all of its H+ in the stomach’s watery environment. This strong acid aids in digestion and kills ingested microbes. Weak acids do not ionize completely; that is, some of their hydrogen ions remain bonded within a compound in solution. An example of a weak acid is vinegar, or acetic acid; it is called acetate after it gives up a proton.

slides.title: Part 3. Acid-Base Balance
slides.body:
Part 3. Acid-Base Balance

A base is a substance that releases hydroxyl ions (OH–) in solution (e.g., NaOH, a strong base) or accepts protons (H+) from solution (e.g., bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻, a weak base)), thus increasing OH- presence indirectly
OH– combines with H+ present to form water (H20)
removes H+ and reduces solution’s acidity
Strong bases release most of their hydroxyl ions; weak bases release only some or accept protons less readily than strong bases

Acids and Bases. (a) In aqueous solution, an acid dissociates into hydrogen ions (H+) and anions. Nearly every molecule of a strong acid dissociates, producing a high concentration of H+. (b) In aqueous solution, a base dissociates into hydroxyl ions (OH–) and cations. Nearly every molecule of a strong base dissociates, producing a high concentration of OH–.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: A base is a substance that releases hydroxyl ions (OH–) in solution, or one that accepts H+ already present in solution. The hydroxyl ions (also known as hydroxide ions) or other basic substances combine with H+ present to form a water molecule, thereby removing H+ and reducing the solution’s acidity. Strong bases release most or all of their hydroxyl ions; weak bases release only some hydroxyl ions or absorb only a few H+

slides.title: Part 3. Acid-Base Balance
slides.body:
Part 3. Acid-Base Balance

pH (“potential of hydrogen”) = relative acidity or alkalinity of a solution
pH 4 solution has 10X higher H+ concentration that pH 5 solution
pH < 7 = acidic
pH 7 = neutral
e.g., pure water
pH > 7 is basic (alkaline)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

The pH Scale.
slides.notes:
The relative acidity or alkalinity of a solution can be indicated by its pH. pH literally means the “potential of hydrogen”. It is a measure of the amount of hydrogen ions present per litre of a solution, expressed in grams. In technical terms, pH is the logarithm of the reciprocal of the hydrogen ion concentration of a solution. This just means that lower values represent a much greater hydrogen concentration than higher numbers. 

As an example, a pH 4 solution has an H+ concentration that is ten times greater than that of a pH 5 solution. That is, a solution with a pH of 4 is ten times more acidic than a solution with a pH of 5. A solution with a pH of 7 is considered neutral—neither acidic nor basic. Pure water has a pH of 7. The lower the number below 7, the more acidic the solution, or the greater the concentration of H+. The concentration of protons (hydrogen ions) at each pH value is 10 times different than the next pH. The higher the number above 7, the more basic (or alkaline) the solution, or the lower the concentration of H+.

slides.title: Part 3. Acid-Base Balance
slides.body:
Part 3. Acid-Base Balance

pH of body’s cells and blood is around 7.35 to 7.45
regulated by respiratory system, urinary system, and buffers released into body fluids
Buffers are solutions of a weak acid and its conjugate base (e.g., carbonic acid and bicarbonate)
can resist sudden changes in the acidity and alkalinity of the body fluids
e.g., during a slight decrease in bodily fluid pH, the buffer—in this case, acting as a weak base—will bind up the excess hydrogen ions
e.g., during an increase in bodily pH, the buffer will act as a weak acid and contribute H+s

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
All cells of the body depend on homeostatic regulation of acid–base balance at a very narrow range of pH between 7.35 to 7.45. The body therefore has several mechanisms for this regulation, involving breathing (since carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid), the excretion of chemicals in urine, and the internal release of chemicals collectively called buffers into body fluids. 

A buffer is a solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base. A buffer can resist sudden changes in the acidity and alkalinity of the body fluids. For example, if there is even a slight decrease below 7.35 in the pH of a bodily fluid, the buffer in the fluid—in this case, acting as a weak base—will bind the excess hydrogen ions. In contrast, if pH rises above 7.45, the buffer will act as a weak acid and contribute hydrogen ions.
